intro: English has several ways to talk about the future, and the choice depends on meaning: a decision made now, a plan made earlier, a prediction from evidence, or a fixed arrangement. Choosing well makes your English sound natural.
objectifs: Tell the difference between a decision made now (will) and an intention decided earlier (be going to).
Tell the difference between a prediction based on opinion (will) and one based on present evidence (be going to).
Use will for offers, promises, refusals and requests, and the present continuous for fixed arrangements.
Avoid using will after when, if and as soon as.

texte: Will + base verb, the same for every subject: I will go, she will go. Contraction 'll (I'll, she'll); negative won't /wəʊnt/ (= will not).
Be going to + base verb: be changes with the subject (I'm going to, he's going to, they're going to). Negative: I'm not going to, she isn't going to. Question: Are you going to…?
In casual speech, going to often sounds like “gonna” /ˈɡɒnə/. Don't write it in careful texts.

lignes: I'm going to call the bank.
Are you going to help him?
Yes, I will. / No, I won't.
Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.

texte: Will = the decision is made at the moment of speaking, often as a reaction. Be going to = the intention existed before; we are announcing a plan.
A simple test: “Had I thought about this before this conversation?” If yes → going to. If no → will.
exemples: The phone's ringing. – I'll get it!
Instant decision.
I'm going to paint my bedroom this weekend. I've bought the paint.
Plan decided earlier (the paint is bought).
It's cold in here. – OK, I'll close the window.
Immediate reaction.
We're going to have a baby in May!
Intention, announced as news.

texte: Will = a prediction based on what you think, believe or know, often with I think, I'm sure, probably, I expect, I don't think. Be going to = a prediction based on present evidence: you can see it coming.
Watch the position of probably: after will (She'll probably win) but before won't (She probably won't win). And we prefer “I don't think he'll come” to “I think he won't come”.
exemples: I think Cameroon will win the match.
Personal opinion.
Look at those clouds! It's going to rain.
Visible evidence: the clouds.
Careful! You're going to fall!
We can see the fall is about to happen.
Prices will probably rise next year.
General forecast; probably after will.

texte: We also use will for actions we do with words: offering help, promising, threatening, refusing, asking for a favour. Going to is not possible here.
Shall I / Shall we…? (mainly British English) makes offers and suggestions or asks for advice: “Shall I open the window?”, “Shall we go?”
Won't can also show refusal, even for things: “The car won't start.”

lignes: I am offering to do it
I won't tell anyone, I promise.
Will you lend me your charger?
Stop that or I'll call the police!

texte: For a plan that is organised, with a date, a time, other people or a ticket, we prefer the present continuous (lesson 50): “I'm meeting Sophie at six.” Going to is possible but says less about the organisation.
Official timetables (trains, classes, films) use the present simple: “The train leaves at 7.15.”
exemples: I'm flying to Montreal on Friday.
Ticket booked: fixed arrangement.
The conference starts at nine tomorrow.
Official schedule: present simple.

sections.titre: After when, if, as soon as: no will
texte: In time and condition clauses (when, as soon as, before, after, until, if), we use the present simple even for the future: “I'll call you when I arrive”, not “when I will arrive”.
This is one of the most common mistakes for learners. The first conditional (next lesson) uses the same rule.
exemples: I'll text you as soon as I get home.
Not “as soon as I will get”.
When she finishes her degree, she's going to work in Abidjan.
Present simple after when.

formule: decision now / opinion → will + verb · plan already decided / visible evidence → be going to + verb
prononciation: 'll is a light, “dark” /l/: I'll /aɪl/, you'll /jʊəl/ or /jɔːl/, we'll /wiːl/, it'll /ˈɪtl/. Don't drop it: “I go” ≠ “I'll go”.
won't /wəʊnt/ (the vowel in “no”) is different from want /wɒnt/. “I won't go” (I refuse / it isn't going to happen) ≠ “I want to go”.
Before a verb, going to often reduces to /ˈɡəʊɪŋ tə/ or “gonna” /ˈɡɒnə/ in casual speech. But not when going means movement: “I'm going to Paris” never becomes “gonna Paris”.
Shall is weak in “Shall we go?”: /ʃəl wi ˈɡəʊ/.
erreurs: The phone is ringing. – I'm going to answer it.
The phone is ringing. – I'll answer it.
A decision made at that moment: will.
I will call you when I will arrive.
I'll call you when I arrive.
After when, as soon as, if: present simple.
Look at the sky! It will rain.
Look at the sky! It's going to rain.
A prediction from visible evidence: going to.
I think he won't come.
I don't think he'll come.
English usually puts the negative on think.
She will probably not to come.
She probably won't come.
No to after will; probably goes before won't.
I go to the dentist tomorrow at 10.
I'm going to the dentist tomorrow at 10.
A fixed appointment: present continuous, not present simple.
Do you help me? It's heavy.
Will you help me? It's heavy.
To ask for a favour: Will you…? / Can you…?

dialogue.contexte: Ottawa, a Friday evening. Sarah and her flatmate Jean-Paul, from Bafoussam, organise their Saturday.
lignes: Present continuous to ask about arrangements.
I'm meeting my cousin at the market at ten. Then I'm going to cook ndolé for everyone.
Sounds great! I'll help you if you like.
Thanks. Oh, look at the sky. It's going to snow tonight.
Then the roads will probably be terrible tomorrow.
Prediction from opinion; probably after will.
Hmm. I'll call my cousin and ask him to come here instead.
Good idea. Shall I buy the vegetables at the corner shop?
Yes, please. I'll send you a list as soon as I finish this call.

mots: plan
What are your plans for the summer?
something you have decided to do
intend
I intend to finish my degree next year.
to have something in your mind as a plan
probably
It will probably be sunny tomorrow.
very likely
promise
I promise I'll be on time.
to say that you will certainly do something
forecast
The forecast says it's going to rain.
a statement about what will happen, especially the weather
definitely
I'll definitely come to your party.
certainly, without any doubt
offer
Thanks for the offer, but I'll manage.
saying you are willing to do something for someone
look like
It looks like it's going to be a long day.
to seem likely
arrangement
I've made arrangements to meet the client.
a plan organised with other people

exercices.consigne: Write the use: instant decision (D), plan (P), prediction from evidence (E), opinion (O) or promise (Pr).
items: I'm going to study law next year.
P
I'll pay you back on Monday, I promise.
Pr
Watch out! That glass is going to fall.
E
I'm hungry. – I'll make you a sandwich.
D
I think the economy will grow next year.
O

exercices.consigne: Complete with will ('ll) or the correct form of be going to.
items: I've bought a ticket. I ___ see the match on Saturday.
am going to ('m going to)
It's dark in here. – I ___ turn on the light.
'll (will)
She's very pale. I think she ___ faint.
is going to
Don't worry, I ___ tell anyone.
won't
We ___ get married next June. We've booked the hall.
are going to
I'll call you when I (will get / get) home.
get
(I'm having / I'll have) dinner with my boss tonight; we booked a table.
I'm having
The film (starts / will be starting) at 8.30 according to the programme.
starts
(Shall / Will) I open the window?
Shall

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I think it won't rain tomorrow.
I don't think it'll rain tomorrow.
As soon as I will know, I'll tell you.
As soon as I know, I'll tell you.
She will to visit us next week.
She will visit us next week. / She's going to visit us next week.
Wait, I'm going to help you with that box!
Wait, I'll help you with that box!

exercices.consigne: Write what you say in each situation, choosing the right future form.
items: Someone knocks at the door. You decide to open it.
I'll go! / I'll get it!
You see dark clouds and tell your friend.
Look at those clouds: it's going to rain.
You tell a friend about your decision to learn Spanish.
I've decided: I'm going to learn Spanish.
Promise to phone your mother after your arrival in Brussels.
I'll phone you when I arrive in Brussels. / I'll call you when I get to Brussels.

exercices.consigne: Write 4–5 sentences: two plans you have already decided (going to or present continuous), one prediction about your country's future (will), and an offer or a promise to a friend (will).
items: Example answer

Next month I'm going to start a new course in project management. On Saturday I'm meeting my old classmates in Dakar. I think more people will work from home in the future. Don't worry about your move: I'll help you carry the boxes, I promise.

a_retenir: Decision made now, offer, promise, request, refusal → will.
Plan already decided → be going to; fixed arrangement → present continuous.
Prediction: opinion → will (I think…, probably); visible evidence → going to.
After when, if, as soon as, before, until: present simple, never will.
Ask yourself: was this decided before I started speaking?
